prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to bring optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 position: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange the case rests on three points that I can check against my own understanding of the physics rather than on the count of supporters. First, the invention is specific: Katori's magic-wavelength condition lets one hold thousands of neutral atoms in a Lamb-Dicke lattice with the trap-induced light shift cancelled on the clock transition, which combines ion-like confinement with the signal-to-noise of an ensemble. Second, the result is reproduced: several independent laboratories and several species now compare lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level, so the achievement does not depend on one group. Third, the attribution maps onto the idea and the decisive realisation with a compact two-name list, and Ye's later work on spin-polarised fermions and on many-body effects in the lattice goes beyond the first demonstration, which is why two names are justified and one is not. As a theorist I add that a clock at this level turns the gravitational redshift over millimetres into a laboratory observable, which is a physical statement and not only an instrument specification. I am aware that several B007 supporters, myself included, moved there after reading the openings, so I have tried to test the case again against B005 and I still find B007 the better-founded choice for this year. The citation I propose names the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice as the rewarded invention, which addresses the chair's question on separating it from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. Optical clocks sit next to two earlier prizes, the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems with its ion clocks, and a sceptic can read lattice clocks as a continuation of a metrology lineage that has been honoured already. I do not think this is correct, since neither earlier prize introduced the many-atom lattice at a magic wavelength, but it is the question the committee will be asked. Second, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Lisdat and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups made real contributions that a two-name citation cannot cover, and the attribution is clean only relative to the other shortlisted candidates, not in absolute terms. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the stated impact is still prospective. I judge this a mild weakness because the accuracy and reproducibility results are already in hand, but a committee member who wanted to wait one or two years for the redefinition would not be unreasonable.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B005 as a clean prediction followed by discovery, argues that reproduced flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology matters more than settling the pairing mechanism, and compares it with the 1987 high-temperature superconductors.
responses.response: I accept the 1987 analogy as a statement about what a prize can reward without a settled mechanism, and I do not hold the open mechanism against B005 by itself. My remaining difficulty is the combination of three things. The citation for the superconductivity would have to be worded very carefully. The first experimental author, Cao, cannot be named within the supplied names, so the experimental credit would rest on the group leader alone. And twist-angle disorder and sample dependence mean that the intrinsic phase diagram is still being sorted out, as you say yourself. Any one of these I could accept. Together they leave B005 with more interpretive and attribution risk than B007 in 2026. I keep it as my first alternative and I would not call a B005 prize unreasonable. If the committee decided to prefer it I would want the citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observation of the correlated and superconducting states, as Danielsson suggests.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B005 and treats the omission of Cao as a recurrent consequence of the three-name limit, not a disqualification, and wants a citation that does not imply a settled mechanism.
responses.response: Your point that the three-name limit regularly leaves out a first author is fair, and I agree that it is not a disqualification on its own. The difference I see is between a first author who is one of several equally strong claimants and a case where the credit is divided across theory (Bistritzer and MacDonald, with Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto before them) and at least three experimental groups beyond Jarillo-Herrero. For B007 the same limit costs us Takamoto, Ludlow and the European groups, but the two credited names still cover the invention and the record-accuracy realisation. On your wording question, a citation restricted to prediction and observation of the phenomena would be the right form for B005 and it would lower my concern about mechanism. It would not change my concern about credit, so I would not move B005 above B007 on that basis.

responses.point: Olsson answered my circuit-QED opening by saying that no other member ranks it in the top three, that the 2004 proposal and first strong-coupling experiment involve at least five people, and that the 2025 prize makes it too close.
responses.response: I agree with your reading and with the numbers, and I have changed my position on B044 for these reasons. Four credited names for three places, with at least five people involved in the early history, is a real attribution problem, and I note that Pearce and I already chose different triples from the same four names. I would add one scientific qualification. The 2025 prize rewarded macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a single circuit, while cQED is about coupling an artificial atom to a resonator for readout and gates, so I do not accept that B044 duplicates it in content. The objection that remains is timing and balance, and that is enough for me to keep B044 only as my second alternative and to discount my own view on it, given that I direct WACQT.

responses.point: Kroll wants the B007 citation built around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation at extreme accuracy, opposes adding a third name, and prefers pairing the clocks only with a clearly distinct achievement if a second part is considered.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and on keeping to two names. A third name from the comb or ion-clock lineage would blur the distinction from 2005 and 2012 that the citation is supposed to make. On a second part, I considered it as the chair asked and I do not find a candidate on the shortlist that is both distinct and mature enough to justify a second part this year. B012 has the 3-4 sigma source-association question and a credit problem inside a large collaboration, and B044 and B006 have the issues I have already described. Without a strong second candidate a second part would add attribution risk without adding scientific strength, so I keep the prize to one part.

responses.point: Lindroth wants Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat treated as uncredited and says that Ye's work on spin-polarised fermion clocks and comparisons goes beyond the first demonstration, which justifies two names and not one.
responses.response: I agree that this is the reason two names are right and a Katori-only citation would be wrong. As a theorist I would put it this way: Katori's proposal and first lattice clock establish the concept, while the accuracy, stability and many-body programme at JILA shows what the concept can do when the interrogation and the density are controlled. On Takamoto, Ludlow and the European groups, I do not see a way to credit them within the rules, and I see no change to the two-name prize that would be better. The honest answer to the chair's question is that their work is real, that it enters through the reproduction at independent laboratories, and that a two-name prize remains defensible because the credited pair cover the invention and the decisive realisation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as a distinct invention or as a continuation of the metrology lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012. I think the former, but I cannot show that the committee will agree.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would make the B007 case stronger, and whether the committee would regard the prospective part of the impact as a reason to delay.
Whether the open pairing mechanism and the Cao omission in B005 are less serious than I judge, in which case B005 would be a reasonable alternative or a stronger first choice for a later year.
My account of priority dates and recent clock-comparison results rests on recalled history, not on verified records.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers, where Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson are colleagues and Anton Frisk Kockum is a frequent co-author. Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. My work on superconducting circuits, circuit and waveguide QED and quantum-computing theory is close to B044 and, to a lesser extent, B031, so I continue to propose that my view on those candidates be discounted and that I recuse myself if either is put to a vote. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or the other B007 contributors, or to the B005, B012 or B006 communities in the supplied profile.
